title: The House of Wisdom Translators
text:
In the eighth and ninth centuries, the Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad and the wealthy families around them paid for one of history's great translation efforts: putting Greek works of philosophy, medicine, mathematics and astronomy into Arabic. The caliph al-Mamun, who ruled from 813 to 833, was among its keenest patrons, and the palace library known as the House of Wisdom, Bayt al-Hikma, became linked to the movement in later memory.

The translators came from many backgrounds. The best known, Hunayn ibn Ishaq, was a Nestorian Christian physician from al-Hira who knew Greek, Syriac and Arabic. He worked with his son Ishaq and his nephew Hubaysh as a kind of workshop. Hunayn described how he hunted for multiple Greek manuscripts of a work, compared them to establish a correct text, and only then translated, often first into Syriac and then into Arabic. He translated most of the works of the Greek physician Galen. Another leading translator was Thabit ibn Qurra, a Sabian from Harran, and Muslim scholars such as the mathematician al-Khwarizmi built new work on what was translated.

The tenth century bookseller Ibn al-Nadim, in his catalog the Fihrist, records a story that al-Mamun was moved to support translation after dreaming of Aristotle.

The works they translated were studied, criticized and extended by scholars across the Islamic world. Centuries later many reached Europe through Latin translations from Arabic.
lesson: Knowledge grows fastest when people of different languages and faiths work together on a shared goal. Careful method and openness to outsiders both matter.
people: Caliph al-Mamun, Hunayn ibn Ishaq, Thabit ibn Qurra, al-Khwarizmi
source: Ibn al-Nadim, Kitab al-Fihrist (987); Dimitri Gutas, Greek Thought, Arabic Culture (1998)
caveat: Historians such as Dimitri Gutas argue the House of Wisdom was mainly a library and that the translation movement was much broader than one institution.
